rv.q: It may be odd, but this Tempest is absolutely in the spirit of Shakespeare’s ‘insubstantial pageant’, as the man himself put it.
The drama feels unsatisfactory when it is entirely sacrificed for the high concept, and possibly bamboozling for someone encountering it for the first time.

But it’s a typically intriguing response that reframes afresh the issues running through it and asks: if theatre is an interactive ritual of repeated storytelling, whose version of the stories are we hearing?

For the audience, in turn, this production is a discombobulating experience in which it isn’t easy to keep track of all the narrative layers or to fully grasp what it means, yet it has a distinctive beauty and theatricality of its own.
Crouch has crafted a compelling reimagining, infused with a rough, melancholy magic that is as irresistible as it is quietly heartbreaking.
It’s a cerebral and uncompromising – but pretty funny!

Jonathan Bailey's coke-snorting Richard II pulses with energy … The 'Bridgerton' star is a fey and capricious monarch in Nicholas Hytner's modern-dress take on Shakespeare's challenging play … Bailey pulses with energy and charisma, which lifts the mood delightfully after all the monochrome men and their moody machinations.
But there’s still a certain pathos that comes with leaving this space, knowing it’ll be quite some time before you see a Shakespeare play that hums with so much mischief and life.
Equal parts haunting and frustrating, sinister and unpredictable, this is a challenging treatment of a familiar play.
Yet despite the many virtues of making this a conceptual experiment rather than an enchanted isle, at the end it feels all too easy to leave it.
